title: After Twenty Years

teacherSummary.text: A man waits in a New York doorway to meet his old friend Jimmy Wells, twenty years to the day after they parted. He tells a patrolling policeman about the plan. A man claiming to be Jimmy arrives, but he is a plainclothes officer who arrests the waiting man, 'Silky' Bob, wanted in Chicago. A note reveals that the patrolman was Jimmy, who recognized Bob as the wanted man and could not arrest him himself.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “After Twenty Years,” how does Henry show friendship tested by duty? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In After Twenty Years, how does Henry develop the idea of friendship tested by duty? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how After Twenty Years develops the idea of friendship tested by duty. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of After Twenty Years (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of friendship tested by duty. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what After Twenty Years suggests about friendship tested by duty. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's irony and foreshadowing), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how O. Henry uses irony in After Twenty Years to complicate the reader's understanding of friendship tested by duty. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate After Twenty Years within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of friendship tested by duty responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read After Twenty Years alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of friendship tested by duty follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to After Twenty Years and its treatment of friendship tested by duty. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's irony and foreshadowing, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads After Twenty Years as evidence for a larger claim about friendship tested by duty in After Twenty Years. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads After Twenty Years as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of friendship tested by duty. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on After Twenty Years.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Would you turn in a friend who had done something seriously wrong? Why or why not? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Nothing in this story needs a special warning.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are submerged, corresponded, egotism, unfolded, vicinity. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “The other, submerged in his overcoat, listened with interest.” In this sentence it means: sink below the surface; go under or as if under water. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of After Twenty Years would have known. Published in 1906 and collected in The Four Million, which names the ordinary New Yorkers O. Henry wrote about. Why does this story matter? A compact surprise ending that rewards rereading for planted clues. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “THE policeman on the beat moved up the avenue impressively.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to friendship tested by duty? I circle “impressively”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find irony, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: THE policeman on the beat moved up the avenue impressively. The impressiveness was habitual and not for show, for spectators were few. The time was barely 10 o’clock at night, but chilly gusts of wind with a taste of rain in them had well nigh depeopled the streets.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Foreshadowing, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how After Twenty Years develops the idea of friendship tested by duty. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to loyalty and duty? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about friendship tested by duty, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes friendship tested by duty. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
